- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., 0.00 or -0.33) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, reduce forecast slope or shift mean downward to reflect bearish sentiment.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., 64.40 → 64.49), model often overcorrects upward; cap forecast growth to avoid overshoot.  
- If event net supply is negative and bearish sentiment dominates, model tends to underreact — adjust forecast downward by 2–5% of recent range.  
- When sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 or negative values, model should not assume continuation of prior trend — reset baseline to recent low or median.  
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome shows strong downward trend after 10–15 days, model often fails to recognize it — apply early mean reversion bias (e.g., drop 1–2% per 3–5 days).  
- If recent auction supply events are frequent (e.g., 3+ per 30d), model tends to overestimate price stability — reduce forecast slope or add downward drift.  
- When bullish sentiment is low but model forecasts remain high, introduce downward bias proportional to bearish event count.  
- If sentiment history shows alternating 0.67/1.00/0.33, model often misinterprets trend — use weighted average of recent sentiment to adjust forecast direction.
